entries.title: Arabs and Arabia: Isaiah 21:13
entries.content:
The argument is that the Bible itself points to the Arabs and to a prophet from among them. Isaiah 21:13 opens an oracle “concerning Arabia”; the Hebrew word for oracle also means a burden, and the reading offered is that a weighty responsibility, the carrying of God’s message to humankind, is laid on the Arabs.

Isaiah 42:11 speaks of the villages Kedar inhabits, and Kedar was a son of Ishmael, so the verse is about Ishmael’s descendants; Ezekiel 27:21 likewise names Arabia and the princes of Kedar. In Deuteronomy 33:2 God shines forth from Mount Paran, which lies in Arabia, with ten thousand holy ones. The reading is that this foretells the coming of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the ten thousand who entered Makkah with him.

Deuteronomy 32:21 is read the same way: God says he will provoke Israel to jealousy with “those who are no people” and anger them with “a foolish nation”. On this reading the nation of no standing is the pre-Islamic Arabs, who were raised up and honoured through a prophet.

The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites.

Isaiah 21:13

He said, “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon us; he shone forth from Mount Paran; he came from the ten thousands of holy ones, with flaming fire at his right hand.

Deuteronomy 33:2

They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

Deuteronomy 32:21

Source: see Credits and references (no. 1, p. 4).

entries.title: Abraham: Genesis 12:19
entries.content:
Two points are made about Abraham (peace be upon him). The first concerns marriage. When Pharaoh rebukes Abram in Genesis 12:19 for saying “She is my sister” so that he took her as his wife, and Abraham admits in Genesis 20:12 that Sarah really is his sister, his father’s daughter, who became his wife, the Bible is shown telling this without embarrassment. Genesis 16:3 adds that Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham “as a wife”. The point is that these are the patriarchs the critic holds up as models, in the very book used to attack Islam’s teaching on marriage.

The second point is a promise that did not come true as stated. God promises Abraham and his offspring all the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession in Genesis 17:8, and says the same in Genesis 13:15 and Exodus 32:13. Yet Acts 7:5 says God gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length. The question put is how an everlasting gift can be said to be given to a man who never owned any of it.

Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife.

Genesis 20:12

And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God.”

Genesis 17:8

Source: see Credits and references (no. 2, p. 4).

entries.title: Absurdities (a): Numbers 22:27-28
entries.content:
The first of a list of passages the argument calls absurd: a donkey speaks to Balaam, Numbers 22:27-28. The point is that a story of an animal holding a conversation with a man is hard to accept as sober history.

When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. And Balaam’s anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff. Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, “What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?”

Numbers 22:27-28

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (b): Leviticus 11:20
entries.content:
Leviticus 11:20 calls winged creatures that go on all fours detestable. The objection is that it describes flying creatures as walking on four legs, which is not how birds are made.

“All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you.

Leviticus 11:20

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (c): Leviticus 12:1
entries.content:
Leviticus 12:1-5 makes a mother unclean for seven days after a son, but for two weeks after a daughter. The complaint is that the birth of a girl is treated as a double defilement, which sits badly with the claim that the book comes from a just God.

“Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If a woman conceives and bears a male child, then she shall be unclean seven days. As at the time of her menstruation, she shall be unclean.

Leviticus 12:2

But if she bears a female child, then she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her menstruation. And she shall continue in the blood of her purifying for sixty-six days.

Leviticus 12:5

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (d): Judges 3:31
entries.content:
Judges 3:31 says Shamgar killed 600 Philistines with an oxgoad, a farmer’s prod. The argument finds the feat too fantastic to take at face value.

After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.

Judges 3:31

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (e): Judges 15:15-16
entries.content:
In Judges 15:15-16 Samson strikes down a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey. It is set beside the previous item as another tale of one man defeating an army with an improvised weapon.

And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men. And Samson said, “With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men.”

Judges 15:15-16

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (f): Revelation 13:1-2
entries.content:
Revelation 13:1-2 describes a beast with seven heads and ten horns that is like a leopard, with feet like a bear’s and a mouth like a lion’s. The argument holds this up as a monstrous picture it finds hard to square with a sober revelation. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (g): 2 Kings 18:27
entries.content:
In 2 Kings 18:27, repeated in Isaiah 36:12, the Assyrian field commander warns that the men on the wall will eat their own dung and drink their own urine. The complaint is that such crude language appears in a book presented as a holy revelation, though it is the enemy’s threat that is quoted.

But the Rabshakeh said to them, “Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and to drink their own urine?”

2 Kings 18:27

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (h): Malachi 2:3
entries.content:
Malachi 2:3 has God threaten to spread dung on the priests’ faces. It is listed for its coarse imagery.

Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and spread dung on your faces, the dung of your offerings, and you shall be taken away with it.

Malachi 2:3

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (i): Ezekiel 4:12-15
entries.content:
Ezekiel 4:12-15 first tells the prophet to bake his bread over human dung, then, when he protests that he has never been defiled, allows cow dung instead. The argument counts the command itself as unfitting for a divine instruction.

And you shall eat it as a barley cake, baking it in their sight on human dung.” And the LORD said, “Thus shall the people of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations where I will drive them.” Then I said, “Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I have never defiled myself. From my youth up till now I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts, nor has tainted meat come into my mouth.” Then he said to me, “See, I assign to you cow’s dung instead of human dung, on which you may prepare your bread.”

Ezekiel 4:12-15

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (j): Judges 16:1
entries.content:
Judges 16:1 says Samson went to Gaza, saw a prostitute and went in to her. The point is that a judge of Israel is shown in this light with no word of rebuke at that spot.

Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.

Judges 16:1

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (k): Ruth 3:4-15
entries.content:
In Ruth 3:4-15 Ruth, on her mother-in-law’s advice, goes at night to the threshing floor and lies down at Boaz’s feet. The argument reads the scene as improper and cites it among the passages it finds unsuitable for family reading.

And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down. At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet!

Ruth 3:7-8

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Absurdities (l): 1 Kings 1:1-4
entries.content:
1 Kings 1:1-4 tells how the aged David could not keep warm, so a beautiful young woman, Abishag, was found to lie beside him and attend him. The argument lists it as David in bed with a young virgin. Note that the same passage says the king “knew her not”.

Now King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm. Therefore his servants said to him, “Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm.” So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king. The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not.

1 Kings 1:1-4

Source: see Credits and references (no. 3, p. 5).

entries.title: Alcohol: Proverbs 31:6-7
entries.content:
Proverbs 31:6-7 advises giving strong drink to the one who is perishing and wine to those in bitter distress, so that they may drink and forget their poverty and their misery. The argument asks whether such counsel can come from God. In the New Testament, 1 Timothy 5:23 tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and take a little wine for his stomach and his frequent illnesses, so that alcohol is recommended in place of water.

The contrast offered is with the Qur’an, which calls intoxicants the handiwork of Satan (Qur’an 5:90), and with the experience of groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous, who treat alcohol as a destroyer of lives.

Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress;

Proverbs 31:6

Source: see Credits and references (no. 4, p. 6).

entries.title: Apostasy: Deuteronomy 13:8
entries.content:
Deuteronomy 13:6-10 covers a person who secretly urges others to serve other gods. In the verses that follow, no pity is to be shown, nothing is to be concealed, and the one who heard the plea must strike first.

The argument is aimed at those who accuse Islam of a harsh penalty for leaving the faith: the same penalty is commanded in their own scripture, and in plain terms.

you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.

Deuteronomy 13:8

But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people.

Deuteronomy 13:9

Source: see Credits and references (no. 5, p. 6).

entries.title: Bastard: Deuteronomy 23:2
entries.content:
Deuteronomy 23:2 bars anyone born of a forbidden union from the assembly of the LORD, and his descendants too, to the tenth generation. Zechariah 9:6 has a mixed people dwelling in Ashdod. The argument is that a person is shut out of the worshipping community for ten generations because of the circumstances of his birth, through no act of his own.

The same theme of birth and legitimacy comes up again in the New Testament in Hebrews 12:8, which says that those without discipline are not true sons.

“No one born of a forbidden union may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of his descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD.

Deuteronomy 23:2

a mixed people shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of Philistia.

Zechariah 9:6

Source: see Credits and references (no. 6, p. 6).

entries.title: Circumcision: Genesis 17:13
entries.content:
Genesis 17:13-14 makes circumcision an everlasting covenant in the flesh, binding on the son born in the house and the slave bought with money, and says any uncircumcised male “shall be cut off from his people”. The argument stresses the word everlasting.

If the covenant is perpetual, the question is on what authority it was set aside, and what it means that the penalty for neglect, being cut off, is so severe.

both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant.

Genesis 17:13

Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant.”

Genesis 17:14

Source: see Credits and references (no. 7, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (a): 2 Samuel 24:1
entries.content:
Who tempted David to count the people? 2 Samuel 24:1 says the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel and he incited David. 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan stood against Israel and incited David. The two accounts name different agents for the same act.

Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, “Go, number Israel and Judah.”

2 Samuel 24:1

Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel.

1 Chronicles 21:1

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (b): 2 Samuel 10:18
entries.content:
After the same battle 2 Samuel 10:18 says David killed the men of 700 chariots and 40,000 horsemen, while 1 Chronicles 19:18 says 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers. The numbers and the kind of troops both differ.

And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there.

2 Samuel 10:18

And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army.

1 Chronicles 19:18

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (c): 1 Kings 7:26
entries.content:
The bronze sea in Solomon’s temple holds two thousand baths in 1 Kings 7:26 but three thousand in 2 Chronicles 4:5.

Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.

1 Kings 7:26

Its thickness was a handbreadth. And its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held 3,000 baths.

2 Chronicles 4:5

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (d): 2 Chronicles 9:25
entries.content:
Solomon’s stalls for horses number 4,000 in 2 Chronicles 9:25 but 40,000 in 1 Kings 4:26, a tenfold gap between two accounts of the same king.

And Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.

2 Chronicles 9:25

Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen.

1 Kings 4:26

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (e): 1 Samuel 28:6
entries.content:
Did Saul ask the LORD for guidance? 1 Samuel 28:6 says he inquired of the LORD and was not answered, so he went to a medium. 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 says he did not seek guidance from the LORD, and that this is why he died. The two accounts of the same episode seem to say he did and he did not.

And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.

1 Samuel 28:6

He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.

1 Chronicles 10:14

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (f): John 3:13
entries.content:
John 3:13 says that no one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down. Against this the Old Testament tells of Elijah, who in 2 Kings 2:11 went up by a whirlwind into heaven, and of Enoch, who in Genesis 5:24 walked with God and was not, for God took him. The argument is that the Gospel statement is contradicted by these earlier ascents.

And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

2 Kings 2:11

Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.

Genesis 5:24

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (g): John 18:9
entries.content:
In John 18:9 Jesus (peace be upon him) is made to say that he lost none of those given to him. In John 17:12 he says he guarded them and that none was lost except the son of destruction, which is one. The argument sets the two sayings side by side as a contradiction in the same Gospel. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: Contradictions (h): 2 Chronicles 6:36
entries.content:
2 Chronicles 6:36 says there is no one who does not sin. 1 John 3:9 says that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning. The argument holds that the two cannot both be taken as stated, for one makes every person a sinner and the other makes the born-again sinless.

“If they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to a land far or near,

2 Chronicles 6:36

Source: see Credits and references (no. 8, p. 7).

entries.title: David: 2 Samuel 11:4
entries.content:
David is called a man after God’s own heart, yet 2 Samuel 11:4 says he sent for Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and lay with her. The argument goes on to the aftermath in 2 Samuel 11:6-25, where David arranges for Uriah to be placed where he will be killed in battle.

A third charge concerns David’s dancing before the ark, treated under the topic of prophets described as naked.

So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house.

2 Samuel 11:4

Source: see Credits and references (no. 9, p. 8).

entries.title: God: qualities attributed to Him (a): Isaiah 5:26
entries.content:
Under the heading of qualities that do not befit God, the first is that he whistles. Isaiah 5:26 has him whistle for a nation from the ends of the earth, Zechariah 10:8 has him whistle for his people to gather them in, and Isaiah 7:18 uses the same image. The argument finds the picture too homely for the Almighty.

He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come!

Isaiah 5:26

“I will whistle for them and gather them in, for I have redeemed them, and they shall be as many as they were before.

Zechariah 10:8

Source: see Credits and references (no. 10, p. 8).

entries.title: God: qualities attributed to Him (b): Isaiah 42:13
entries.content:
A God who roars. Isaiah 42:13 has the LORD cry out and shout aloud like a man of war, and Jeremiah 25:30 says he will roar from on high against his fold. The images are set down as unworthy of the divine.

The LORD goes out like a mighty man, like a man of war he stirs up his zeal; he cries out, he shouts aloud, he shows himself mighty against his foes.

Isaiah 42:13

“You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: “‘The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.

Jeremiah 25:30

Source: see Credits and references (no. 10, p. 8).

entries.title: God: qualities attributed to Him (c): Isaiah 7:20
entries.content:
Isaiah 7:20 says the Lord will shave with a hired razor, the king of Assyria, taking the hair of the head and feet and the beard. It is listed as the picture of God as a barber.

In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River—with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also.

Isaiah 7:20

Source: see Credits and references (no. 10, p. 8).

entries.title: God: qualities attributed to Him (d): Jeremiah 15:6
entries.content:
A God who repents. In Genesis 6:6 the LORD regretted that he had made man and was grieved, and in Jeremiah 15:6 he says he is weary of relenting. The argument holds that regret implies a lack of foreknowledge, which is not a quality of God.

You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting.

Jeremiah 15:6

And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.

Genesis 6:6

Source: see Credits and references (no. 10, p. 8).

entries.title: God: qualities attributed to Him (e): 2 Samuel 22:11
entries.content:
2 Samuel 22:11 says he rode on a cherub and flew. The picture of God riding a creature is another entry in the list of descriptions the argument calls unfit.

He rode on a cherub and flew; he was seen on the wings of the wind.

2 Samuel 22:11

Source: see Credits and references (no. 10, p. 8).

entries.title: God: qualities attributed to Him (f): 1 Samuel 6:19
entries.content:
1 Samuel 6:19 says the LORD struck down some of the men of Beth-shemesh because they looked upon the ark, and the people mourned the great blow. The argument objects to a God who kills people merely for looking into a box.

And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow.

1 Samuel 6:19

Source: see Credits and references (no. 10, p. 8).

entries.title: God with a small "g": 2 Corinthians 4:4
entries.content:
Hebrew, Greek and Arabic do not have separate capital and lowercase letters in the way English does, so whether a word is printed God or god is a decision by the translator. The argument is that translators have used that freedom to suit their doctrine.

In 2 Corinthians 4:4 the “god of this age” who blinds unbelievers is the Devil, and in Exodus 7:1 God says he has made Moses like God to Pharaoh, so the same word is applied to a creature. Yet when John 1:1 uses the same word for the Word, the capital letter is chosen. The point is that the same Greek word is printed one way for the Devil and Moses and another way for Jesus (peace be upon him).

And the LORD said to Moses, “See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet.

Exodus 7:1

Source: see Credits and references (no. 11, p. 8).

entries.title: God: seeing God: John 1:18
entries.content:
The Bible says in John 1:18 and 1 Timothy 6:16 that no one has seen God or can see him, and Exodus 33:20 says no man can see God’s face and live.

Yet other passages say the opposite. In Exodus 33:11 the LORD speaks to Moses face to face as a man to his friend; in Exodus 24:10 Moses, Aaron and seventy elders saw the God of Israel; and in Genesis 32:30 Jacob says he has seen God face to face and lived. Exodus 33:23 adds that God would let Moses see his back. The argument sets these side by side as flat contradiction about God’s nature.

But,” he said, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live.”

Exodus 33:20

Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. When Moses turned again into the camp, his assistant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent.

Exodus 33:11

and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness.

Exodus 24:10

So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, “For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.”

Genesis 32:30

Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen.”

Exodus 33:23

Source: see Credits and references (no. 12, p. 9).

entries.title: God: confusion and evil: 1 Corinthians 14:33
entries.content:
1 Corinthians 14:33 says God is not a God of confusion. The argument sets against it Isaiah 45:7, where God says he forms light, creates darkness, makes well-being and creates calamity, and 1 Samuel 16:14, where a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented Saul. It adds 2 Thessalonians 2:11, which says God sends a strong delusion so that people believe a lie.

The complaint is that the Bible makes God the author of calamity and deception while insisting he is not the author of confusion.

I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things.

Isaiah 45:7

Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him.

1 Samuel 16:14

Source: see Credits and references (no. 13, p. 10).

entries.title: God: further contradictions (a): Mark 10:27
entries.content:
The Gospels have Jesus (peace be upon him) say that with God all things are possible, in Mark 10:27 and Matthew 19:26. Judges 1:19 reports that the LORD was with Judah, and Judah took the hill country, but could not drive out the people of the plain because they had chariots of iron. The argument asks how an almighty God is stopped by iron chariots.

And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron.

Judges 1:19

Source: see Credits and references (no. 14, p. 10).

entries.title: God: further contradictions (b): Psalms 30:5
entries.content:
Psalm 30:5 says God’s anger lasts only a moment, while Numbers 32:13 says his anger kept Israel wandering in the wilderness for forty years until the generation that did evil had died out. The point put is that a moment and forty years cannot both describe the same anger.

For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.

Psalms 30:5

And the LORD’s anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone.

Numbers 32:13

Source: see Credits and references (no. 14, p. 10).

entries.title: God: further contradictions (c): Numbers 23:19
entries.content:
Numbers 23:19 says God is not a man that he should change his mind. Yet 1 Samuel 15:35 says the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king, and Exodus 32:14 says he relented from the disaster he had spoken of. The argument treats these as a direct clash about whether God ever changes course.

God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?

Numbers 23:19

And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

1 Samuel 15:35

And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.

Exodus 32:14

Source: see Credits and references (no. 14, p. 10).

entries.title: God: further contradictions (d): Psalms 100:5
entries.content:
Psalm 100:5 says God’s steadfast love endures forever. In 1 Samuel 15:3 Saul is commanded to strike Amalek and devote everything to destruction, sparing neither man nor woman, child nor infant, nor even the animals. The argument asks how that command fits with a love that never ends.

For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations.

Psalms 100:5

Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’”

1 Samuel 15:3

Source: see Credits and references (no. 14, p. 10).

entries.title: God: further contradictions (e): 1 Timothy 6:16
entries.content:
1 Timothy 6:16 says God lives in unapproachable light, while Solomon says in 1 Kings 8:12 that the LORD has said he would dwell in thick darkness. The argument puts light and thick darkness side by side as contradictory descriptions of where God dwells.

Then Solomon said, “The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.

1 Kings 8:12

Source: see Credits and references (no. 14, p. 10).

entries.title: God: further contradictions (f): James 1:13
entries.content:
James 1:13 says God tempts no one. Genesis 22:1 says God tested Abraham by commanding him to offer his son. The argument notes that the two passages use different words, test and tempt, but treats the test of Abraham as the very thing James says God does not do.

After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, “Abraham!” And he said, “Here I am.”

Genesis 22:1

Source: see Credits and references (no. 14, p. 10).

entries.title: Holy Ghost: Luke 1:15
entries.content:
Many Christian groups claim to possess the gift of the Holy Spirit as their own. The argument questions how special that gift can be when it is claimed so widely, and then raises a puzzle from the Gospels. Luke 1:15 says John the Baptist would be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, Luke 1:41 and 1:67 say the same of Elizabeth and Zechariah, and John 20:22 has Jesus (peace be upon him) breathe on his disciples and tell them to receive it. Yet Jesus himself is described as receiving the Spirit only at his baptism, in Matthew 3:16, some thirty years after his birth. Why, the argument asks, would he be last?

Mark 3:29 warns that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is never forgiven. The reading offered is that the Holy Spirit in these sayings is a reference to the coming of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Author's note: HOLY GHOST: The words "Holy Ghost" here, should read the "HOLY SPIRIT," a reference to the Holy Prophet of Islam, the Holy Prophet Muhummed (pbuh). For a detailed exposition obtain the FREE copy of my Book - "Muhummed (pbuh) the Natural Successor to Christ (pbuh)."

entries.title: Incest: Genesis 19:33-35
entries.content:
The argument defines incest as sexual relations between people too closely related, and says the Bible records several cases without condemning them. It begins with Genesis 19:33-35, where Lot’s two daughters get their father drunk and each lies with him in turn so that they may have children by him.

It continues with Reuben lying with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, in Genesis 35:22, and Judah sleeping with his daughter-in-law Tamar, who had disguised herself as a prostitute, in Genesis 38:15-18. It adds Amnon’s assault on his half-sister Tamar in 2 Samuel 13:11-14, where she begs him not to do such an outrageous thing, and Absalom taking his father’s concubines in public in 2 Samuel 16:22.

Leviticus 18:8-18 forbids all of these unions, which makes the narratives stand out. The question raised is why scripture reports such episodes so plainly and what lesson it draws from them.

So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father. He did not know when she lay down or when she arose. The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, “Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father.” So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.

Genesis 19:33-35

While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine. And Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.

Genesis 35:22

But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.

2 Samuel 13:14

So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.

2 Samuel 16:22

Author's note: CONCUBINE and WIFE are synonymous terms in the Bible. Look for it in the index under "KETURAH" (the third wife of Abraham).

entries.title: Israelites: Ezekiel 16:28
entries.content:
The prophets often describe Israel’s unfaithfulness to God in the language of an unfaithful wife, and this entry collects those passages. Ezekiel 16:28 says Jerusalem played the whore with the Assyrians and still was not satisfied. Ezekiel 23 retells the story as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, standing for Samaria and Jerusalem, who give themselves to foreign lovers. Hosea 4:12 says a spirit of whoredom has led the people astray so that they left their God, and the theme returns in Hosea 6:10 and 9:1.

The argument reads these as a record of Israel’s repeated rebellion, and also asks whether such explicit imagery is fitting in a book offered as the word of God.

You played the whore also with the Assyrians, because you were not satisfied; yes, you played the whore with them, and still you were not satisfied.

Ezekiel 16:28

My people inquire of a piece of wood, and their walking staff gives them oracles. For a spirit of whoredom has led them astray, and they have left their God to play the whore.

Hosea 4:12

Source: see Credits and references (no. 17, p. 16).

entries.title: Jeremiah: Jeremiah 1:5
entries.content:
Jeremiah 1:5 has God say that before he formed Jeremiah in the womb he knew him, and that he appointed him a prophet to the nations. The argument sets this beside Jeremiah’s complaint in Jeremiah 20:7 that the LORD has deceived him and that he was deceived. A prophet chosen before birth is hard to reconcile with a God who is said to deceive that same prophet.

“Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”

Jeremiah 1:5

O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me.

Jeremiah 20:7

Source: see Credits and references (no. 18, p. 16).

entries.title: Jesus (pbuh): John 2:9
entries.content:
A string of observations about Jesus (peace be upon him) in the Gospels, offered as evidence that he was a prophet and not God. His first miracle in John 2 is turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana; in the Qur’an (19:29-33) his first miracle is speaking as a baby to clear his mother’s name. He speaks sharply to the religious leaders in Matthew 16:4 and Matthew 23, calling them hypocrites, whitewashed tombs and a brood of vipers. He addresses his mother as “woman” in John 2:4, the same word he uses to the woman brought before him in John 8:10, and says in Luke 12:49-51 that he came to bring fire and division, not peace.

He turns away the man who calls him good in Matthew 19:16-17, saying that only God is good. His authority is something he was given (Matthew 28:18); he says he can do nothing on his own (John 5:30); he casts out demons by the finger of God (Luke 11:20); and before raising Lazarus he thanks the Father for hearing him, saying he speaks aloud so the crowd may believe (John 11:41-43). Peter calls him a man whom God attested by the miracles God did through him (Acts 2:22). Finally, in Matthew 26:7-11 he defends the woman who poured costly ointment on him against his disciples’ complaint that it should have gone to the poor, which the argument reads as strange for a teacher of self-denial.

Taken together, the argument says these sayings describe a human messenger dependent on God. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Author's note: "Small "g": See in the index for "GOD" with a small "g".

entries.title: Jesus (pbuh): power and knowledge: John 5:30
entries.content:
The points collected here concern the humanity of Jesus (peace be upon him) in the Gospels, and are offered as reasons to doubt that he is God. In John 5:30 he says he can do nothing on his own. In Mark 13:32 he says that no one knows the day or the hour, not even the Son, but only the Father. In Mark 11:13 he goes to a fig tree looking for fruit, and finds none because it was not the season.

He says he is thirsty in John 19:28, he weeps in John 11:35, and in Mark 1:13 he is tempted by Satan for forty days. The argument asks how someone who lacks knowledge, tires, thirsts, weeps and is tempted can be the all-knowing God who cannot be tempted. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 20, p. 20).

entries.title: Jesus (pbuh): the mission to Israel: Matthew 10:5-6
entries.content:
In Matthew 10:5-6 Jesus (peace be upon him) sends out the twelve and tells them not to go to the Gentiles or enter a Samaritan town, but to go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. In Matthew 15:24-26 he tells the Canaanite woman who asks him to heal her daughter that he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, and that it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.

The argument takes these sayings as plain evidence that his mission was to the Jews alone, which is hard to square with a message to all nations. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Author's note: See the word "WORSHIP" in the Index.

entries.title: Jesus (pbuh): sundry points: Matthew 10:23
entries.content:
A set of sayings of Jesus (peace be upon him) that the argument finds troubling. In Matthew 10:23 he tells the disciples they will not have gone through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes; two thousand years later, nothing of the kind has happened. In Mark 4:11-12 he explains that he speaks in parables so that those outside will see and not perceive, lest they turn and be forgiven, which the argument reads as concealing his message. In Luke 14:26 he says anyone who does not hate father, mother, wife and children cannot be his disciple.

John 14:6 has him say that no one comes to the Father except through him, but Peter says in Acts 10:34-35 that in every nation anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him. The argument sets the two sayings in tension. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 22, p. 21).

entries.title: Jews: Deuteronomy 9:24
entries.content:
The Bible itself describes Israel as a people who rebelled again and again. Moses tells them in Deuteronomy 9:24 that they have been rebellious from the day he knew them, and in Deuteronomy 31:27 that they are rebellious and stubborn, and will be more so after his death. Deuteronomy 28:68 warns that the LORD will bring them back to Egypt in ships to be sold as slaves with no buyer, and Hosea 8:13 says that God will remember their iniquity, punish their sins, and that they shall return to Egypt.

Matthew 21:43, in which Jesus (peace be upon him) says the kingdom of God will be taken from his hearers and given to a people producing its fruits, is taken to mean that another community would take their place. The argument is a reading of what scripture says about Israel’s record and its consequences. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.

Deuteronomy 9:24

For I know how rebellious and stubborn you are. Behold, even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious against the LORD. How much more after my death!

Deuteronomy 31:27

And the LORD will bring you back in ships to Egypt, a journey that I promised that you should never make again; and there you shall offer yourselves for sale to your enemies as male and female slaves, but there will be no buyer.”

Deuteronomy 28:68

As for my sacrificial offerings, they sacrifice meat and eat it, but the LORD does not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins; they shall return to Egypt.

Hosea 8:13

Source: see Credits and references (no. 23, p. 22).

entries.title: Keturah: Genesis 25:1
entries.content:
Genesis 25:1 says Abraham took another wife, Keturah, but 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her Abraham’s concubine. The argument notes that a wife and a concubine are not the same thing, so the two books describe her status differently.

Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.

Genesis 25:1

The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan.

1 Chronicles 1:32

Source: see Credits and references (no. 24, p. 23).

entries.title: Massacre: Numbers 31:17-18
entries.content:
The argument gathers the passages in which Israel is told to wipe out whole populations. In Numbers 31:17-18 Moses orders every male child and every woman who has been with a man to be killed, while the young girls are kept alive for the Israelites, and the count of these in Numbers 31:35 comes to 32,000. Deuteronomy 20:16 says that in the cities given as an inheritance nothing that breathes is to be left alive.

Joshua 6:21 reports that at Jericho every man, woman, child, ox, sheep and donkey was devoted to destruction, and Joshua 10:28 says that at Makkedah Joshua left no one remaining. The argument is that a book which commands and reports this has no standing to accuse others of cruelty.

Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him. But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.

Numbers 31:17-18

But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes,

Deuteronomy 20:16

Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.

Joshua 6:21

Source: see Credits and references (no. 25, p. 24).

entries.title: Melchisedek: Hebrews 7:3
entries.content:
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, appears in Genesis 14:18 with bread and wine. Hebrews 7:3 says of him that he has no father, no mother, no genealogy, no beginning of days and no end of life. The argument observes that these are qualities which belong to God alone, and that on this description the priest of Salem outranks Jesus (peace be upon him), who had a mother and a lineage. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.)

Genesis 14:18

Source: see Credits and references (no. 26, p. 24).

entries.title: Messiah: Genesis 31:13
entries.content:
Messiah is an ordinary Hebrew word meaning anointed one, and Christ is simply its Greek counterpart. The argument shows how widely the Old Testament uses it. In Genesis 31:13 God recalls the pillar Jacob anointed at Bethel; in Leviticus 8:10 Moses anoints the tabernacle with the anointing oil; 1 Samuel 2:10 speaks of the horn of God’s anointed king; Ezekiel 28:14 speaks of an anointed guardian cherub.

Isaiah 45:1 goes furthest, for there the LORD calls Cyrus, a pagan king, his anointed. If the word covers a pillar, oil, a cherub and a foreign ruler, the argument says, then being called Messiah does not by itself mark anyone as divine.

I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. Now arise, go out from this land and return to the land of your kindred.’”

Genesis 31:13

Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed:

Isaiah 45:1

Source: see Credits and references (no. 27, p. 24).

entries.title: Muhummed (pbuh): 1 John 4:2
entries.content:
Three claims are made that the Bible speaks of Muhammad (peace be upon him). First, 1 John 4:2 says every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; the Qur’an (3:45) also calls Jesus the Messiah, so a prophet who confesses this fits the test.

Second, in Song of Solomon 5:16 the Hebrew word that the ESV renders “altogether desirable” is argued to be the name Muhammad with a plural-of-respect ending. Third, in John 14:16 Jesus promises “another” helper to be with his followers for ever; the argument says another of the same kind must be a man like Jesus, not a spirit. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

Song of Solomon 5:16

Source: see Credits and references (no. 28, p. 25).

entries.title: Onanism: Genesis 38:8-9
entries.content:
Genesis 38:8-9 tells how Judah told Onan to go in to his dead brother’s wife and raise up offspring for his brother, and how Onan, knowing the child would not be his, wasted his semen on the ground. This is the passage behind the word onanism. The argument lists it among the passages in which the Bible speaks of sexual matters very openly.

Then Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother.” But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he went in to his brother’s wife he would waste the semen on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.

Genesis 38:8-9

Source: see Credits and references (no. 29, p. 26).

entries.title: Paul: 2 Corinthians 12:16
entries.content:
In 2 Corinthians 12:16 Paul answers the charge that he burdened the Corinthians, and says he was crafty and caught them by deceit. The argument takes the verse as Paul’s own admission of cunning and guile, treating the words as a confession of a method rather than a charge he is refuting. The surrounding verses show he is answering a charge made against him, so the verse should be read in context. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Author's note: GUILE: means ruse, sharp practice, treachery, trickery and wiliness.

entries.title: Polygamy: 1 Kings 11:3
entries.content:
1 Kings 11:3 says Solomon had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. The argument adds that Abraham, Jacob and David also had more than one wife, and that the Bible never forbids having several wives as such. The criticism recorded of Solomon is that his wives turned his heart away, not the number of them. The point is that critics who object to plural marriage in Islam are objecting to something their own scripture allows.

He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart.

1 Kings 11:3

Source: see Credits and references (no. 32, p. 27).

entries.title: Prophecies: Genesis 2:17
entries.content:
In Genesis 2:17 God warns Adam that on the day he eats of the tree he shall surely die. Yet Genesis 5:5 says Adam lived 930 years. In Genesis 3:4 the serpent tells Eve that she will not surely die. The argument says that on a plain reading the threat was not carried out when stated and the serpent’s word was nearer the facts, unless “in the day” is stretched to mean centuries later.

but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.”

Genesis 2:17

Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.

Genesis 5:5

But the serpent said to the woman, “You will not surely die.

Genesis 3:4

Source: see Credits and references (no. 33, p. 27).

entries.title: Prophets (but naked): Genesis 9:21
entries.content:
A list of cases in which people of God appear unclothed. Noah drinks wine and lies uncovered in his tent in Genesis 9:21. Saul strips off his clothes, prophesies, and lies naked all day and night in 1 Samuel 19:24. David is mocked by Michal in 2 Samuel 6:20 for uncovering himself before his servants’ maids. In Isaiah 20:3-4 the LORD tells Isaiah to walk naked and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt.

The argument asks whether such conduct suits those held up as examples to the faithful.

He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent.

Genesis 9:21

And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

1 Samuel 19:24

Then the LORD said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt.

Isaiah 20:3-4

Source: see Credits and references (no. 34, p. 28).

entries.title: Rape: 2 Samuel 13:14
entries.content:
Two cases within David’s own household. In 2 Samuel 13:14 Amnon, being stronger than his half-sister Tamar, violates her and lies with her. In 2 Samuel 16:22 Absalom pitches a tent on the roof and goes in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. The argument puts both on record as sexual crimes inside the royal family of a king described as a man after God’s heart.

But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.

2 Samuel 13:14

So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.

2 Samuel 16:22

Source: see Credits and references (no. 35, p. 29).

entries.title: Sabbath: Exodus 31:17
entries.content:
Exodus 31:17 says that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed. The argument takes this to mean God grew tired, and sets against it the Qur’an’s teaching (2:255) that the throne of God extends over the heavens and the earth and that guarding them does not weary him.

It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.’”

Exodus 31:17

Source: see Credits and references (no. 36, p. 29).

entries.title: Sarah: Genesis 21:1-2
entries.content:
The argument raises an objection to the language of the Bible about conception. Genesis 21:1-2 says the LORD visited Sarah as he had promised and she conceived Isaac, and Luke 1:35 tells Mary that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the power of the Most High overshadow her. It claims that this way of speaking brings God into the act of conception in terms that suggest a physical role, which it considers unfitting. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised. And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.

Genesis 21:1-2

Source: see Credits and references (no. 37, p. 30).

entries.title: Slavery: Leviticus 25:46
entries.content:
Leviticus 25:46 allows the Israelites to take slaves from the surrounding nations, to leave them to their sons as property, and to hold them as slaves for ever, while forbidding Israelites to rule over one another ruthlessly. The argument says this means slavery is something the Bible sanctions as God’s own law, passed down in families and lasting for life.

You may bequeath them to your sons after you to inherit as a possession forever. You may make slaves of them, but over your brothers the people of Israel you shall not rule, one over another ruthlessly.

Leviticus 25:46

Source: see Credits and references (no. 38, p. 30).

entries.title: Sodomy: Romans 1:25-27
entries.content:
Romans 1:24-27 connects idolatry with what follows: because people exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshipped created things, God gave them up to dishonourable passions, and women and men exchanged natural relations for those that are not. The argument draws attention to the fact that the New Testament explains same-sex desire as a consequence of idolatry, and presents it as a divine judgement. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 39, p. 30).

entries.title: Sons of God: Luke 3:38
entries.content:
The title Son of God is applied to many in the Bible, and the argument uses this to say it cannot prove that Jesus (peace be upon him) is God. Luke 3:38 calls Adam the son of God; Genesis 6:2 speaks of the sons of God who took wives from the daughters of men; Exodus 4:22 calls Israel God’s firstborn son; Jeremiah 31:9 says Ephraim is his firstborn; Psalm 2:7 has God say to the king, “today I have begotten you”; and Romans 8:14 calls all who are led by the Spirit of God sons of God.

Two further questions are put: how can both Israel and Ephraim be firstborn, and how could God beget David on a particular day when David was a grown man? (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.

Genesis 6:2

Then you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son,

Exodus 4:22

I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.

Psalms 2:7

Author's note: TONS: A ton is 2000 lbs weight, that is about a thousand kilograms

entries.title: Swine: Leviticus 11:8
entries.content:
Leviticus 11:8 forbids eating pork or touching the carcasses of pigs, which are unclean. In Mark 5:13 Jesus (peace be upon him) allows the unclean spirits to enter a herd of about two thousand pigs, which then rush down a slope and drown in the sea. The argument asks what the herd’s owners lost, and why a herd should be destroyed to heal one man. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you.

Leviticus 11:8

Source: see Credits and references (no. 41, p. 32).

entries.title: Women: 1 Corinthians 14:34-35
entries.content:
1 Corinthians 14:34-35 says that women should keep silent in the churches and, if they wish to learn, ask their husbands at home, because it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. The argument cites it to show that the New Testament silences women in public worship, which it contrasts with the way Islam treats women. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 43, p. 32).

entries.title: Worship: Mark 5:6
entries.content:
In Mark 5:6 the man with an unclean spirit sees Jesus (peace be upon him) from far off, runs and worships him. Luke 8:28 describes the same event by saying he fell down before him. The argument concludes that the word translated worship can mean showing respect or reverence to someone, and does not by itself prove that Jesus was being treated as God. (The New Testament text is not yet on this site.)

Source: see Credits and references (no. 44, p. 32).
